description: Classifies every public CNA C API declaration on two independent axes. The first is purpose: rules are matched in order against a declaration's header and name and the first match wins, so every route lands in exactly one purpose category and UNEXPLAINED must stay at zero -- a route with no rule is a route nobody has decided about. The second is reachability: which backends actually import the route, measured from the Node adapter's C source and the WebAssembly backend's route table rather than declared here. The two are orthogonal on purpose, because "what is this route for" and "can a consumer reach it today" are different questions and conflating them hides both.

categories.XNA_BACKING: backs an XNA 4.0 member this package projects, reached through a different route or an exact managed implementation
categories.CNA_EXTENSION_BACKING: modern CNA surface outside Microsoft.Xna.Framework, the target of cna-ts/extensions
categories.INTERNAL_RUNTIME_ONLY: runtime plumbing the binding never exposes as public API
categories.MANAGED_BY_DESIGN: XNA value semantics kept exact in TypeScript; routing their *evaluation* through native would add ownership and error paths XNA does not have. A few are still reached where a compiled asset decodes into one.
categories.TOOLING_ONLY: test, diagnostic and fuzzing hooks that are not application surface
categories.INTENTIONALLY_DEFERRED: real XNA 4.0 surface this package has measured and not yet projected
categories.UPSTREAM_RUNTIME_UNAVAILABLE: declared by the ABI but with no runtime that answers it on a locally buildable backend

rules.reason: an explicitly test-only extension hook

XNA's math, geometry, curve, colour and packed-value semantics are deterministic and are implemented exactly in TypeScript; the differential corpus pins them against the reference implementation. Calling native to *evaluate* them would add a handle, an error path and a backend dependency to operations XNA performs with no failure mode at all. Note that purpose is not reachability: thirteen of these routes are reached, because `cna_cnb_decode_curve` hands back a native curve and the only way to lift it into the managed one is to read its loop modes and its keys. The native object is released inside that call and the curve a consumer holds still evaluates in TypeScript.
canonical CNA surface with no Microsoft.Xna.Framework counterpart; it belongs under cna-ts/extensions and never inside the strict XNA projection

the error code of the last failed join, which only means something once a session can be joined -- and joining needs a signed-in gamer this host does not have. Deferred with net_sessions.h, for its reason

PacketReader, PacketWriter, NetworkSessionProperties and QualityOfService are value types with no network in them, and this package implements all four exactly: the packet types extend its own BinaryReader and BinaryWriter, and the property bag is XNA's eight slots where null means "do not match". They are deterministic data structures, so routing them through native would add a handle, an error path and a backend dependency to operations that need none -- the same reason the math types stay managed. Nothing here is blocked by the absence of a network

backs NetworkSession, NetworkGamer and the session collections. Not blocked by CNA: measured, a session is created successfully on this host, both Local and SystemLink, and reports its state and that it is the host. It is blocked by what a session needs first -- at least one signed-in gamer. This host has none, and the only route that produces one is cna_signed_in_gamer_create_ext, which CNA's header describes as the hook for a *platform layer* to publish a gamer. A binding calling it would be inventing the player, and every session claim built on that would be false. The strict surface keeps refusing with GamerServicesNotAvailableException, which is what XNA raises where there is no service

backs the Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Net session surface, which is projected at zero structural differences and refuses at runtime: a NetworkSession needs a signed-in gamer and a peer, and fabricating either would be worse than the exception XNA raises where the platform is absent

backs the projected Microsoft.Xna.Framework.GamerServices types; the adapter reaches this family through the dispatcher's lifetime and the Guide's state, so the rest of it is surface behind an API this package publishes rather than an unbound family
rules.unreachedReason: backs projected GamerServices surface in a header the adapter imports nothing from, so the whole family is measured and deferred rather than partially covered

rules.reason: an _ext route is CNA surface beyond XNA 4.0 by the ABI's own naming rule
the ABI version query is the first route every backend loads and the gate that rejects an incompatible library; it is never public API

an infinite-perspective projection, declared in models.h because glTF cameras need it but a pure matrix routine with no XNA 4.0 counterpart -- XNA's Matrix has no infinite-far-plane perspective at all

SkinningData and AnimationPlayer are the XNA Skinned Model *Sample's* types, not Microsoft.Xna.Framework members -- there is no such class in any XNA 4.0 reference assembly, which is why they carry a content type name of their own. They are CNA extension surface and belong under cna-ts/extensions if they are ever projected, never inside the strict XNA namespace

modern model surface with no XNA 4.0 counterpart: glTF import diagnostics, cameras, skins, material variants, morph targets, GPU-skinned models, named animation clips and the content-tag dictionary. XNA's Model carries none of these -- it has bones, meshes, parts and a tag, and nothing else -- so projecting them into Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Graphics.Model would break the strict contract these gates exist to hold

backs Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Graphics.ModelMeshPart. Ten of these are imported: a managed part lends CNA a native view of itself, built over the vertex and index buffers it already owns rather than over copies, so that CNA's instanced renderer and LOD selection can take a real part. The rest are the setters -- num_vertices, primitive_count, start_index, vertex_offset -- which the managed part exposes as readonly, exactly as XNA does, so there is nothing for them to set. See docs/native-model-graph.md

backs Model, ModelMesh, ModelBone and their collections, all of which this package implements exactly in TypeScript from the XNB readers. These routes are a *parallel* native model graph rather than the backing of the managed one, and adopting them wholesale would give one logical model two owners: CNA's own getters mint a fresh owned handle on every call (measured -- reading one part out of a collection twice yields two different handles, neither equal to the original), so a native graph cannot even preserve the stable object identity the managed graph already has. Deferred deliberately, not for want of measurement; the one place a native object is genuinely needed -- a part handle for the engine extensions -- is covered by the side-car above without duplicating a byte of geometry

loads a Model through CNA's own native content manager. Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Content.ContentManager here is the managed XNB reader stack, with its own cache and its own asset identity; routing Model loads through a second, native cache would give one asset two owners and two identities. It belongs to the native content extension question, not to the strict ContentManager

CNA's content *survey*: scan a content root and report which assets are there and which XNB readers each one needs. XNA has no manifest of any kind, so this is extension surface rather than backing for a Microsoft.Xna.Framework member, and it is projected as cna-ts/extensions/content ContentSurvey. It creates no asset, no cache and no second owner -- which is exactly why it can be projected while the load routes below cannot

backs ContentManager.Load and Unload, which this package implements as a managed XNB reader stack with its own cache. Deliberately not projected: CNA's content manager has a cache and an asset identity of its own, so routing loads through it would give one asset two owners, two identities and two lifetimes, and Load returning the same reference for the same key -- which XNA guarantees and this package's tests pin -- could no longer be stated about either. The architecture decision is written up in docs/native-content-survey.md

CNA's own content extensions -- foreign asset loading, the .cnj loader registry and the game's native content-manager slot. The loader registry only pays off once assets are retrieved *through* the native manager, which is the second cache the load routes are deferred for; it is deferred with them rather than projected as a registration nothing can then load

the rest of CNA's ContentManager surface -- asset-path and normalized-key arithmetic, the service provider, the graphics device and the built-in loader registration. Each backs a ContentManager member this package implements managed, against its own cache; none can be adopted piecemeal without the native manager the load routes are deferred for

asks CNA's reader registry whether it can read a CLR reader name. Imported, because the content survey's whole value is answering "does anything read this?" and CNA's registry is one of the two answers -- this package's own reader registrations are the other
CNA's reflective object dictionary and its extensions to the reader stack; no XNA 4.0 counterpart

CNA's own XNB reader stack -- ContentReader, ContentTypeReaderManager, the reflective and enum readers, and the known-unsupported registry. This package reads XNB in TypeScript and exposes its own reader registration point, so these are a *parallel* implementation of the same format rather than the backing of this one. Adopting them would mean one asset decoded by two stacks, and would need the native ContentManager that content.h's load routes are deferred for. The survey deliberately reads only headers, never payloads, so it needs none of them

the clipboard, the attached-device inventory and a combined power reading. XNA 4.0 has none of these -- no clipboard type, no device enumeration, and no power API outside Windows Phone -- so they are extension surface. What makes them worth binding rather than leaving to devices.h is that CNA does *not* gate them on its extended device layer: measured on a CNA built with CNA_DEVICES=OFF, the clipboard round-trips exactly, one mouse and one keyboard are enumerated by name, and the power route reports a real battery percentage while all three cna_power_get_*_ext routes answer NOT_SUPPORTED. CNA's own header states that it deliberately does not duplicate the clipboard *reads* into the extension layer, which is why writing was reachable here before reading was

sensor enumeration, reached through sensors.h's own routes instead -- this package projects accelerometer and gyroscope there, and a second enumeration of the same devices would answer the same thing by a different name

POD initialisers and comparators for two descriptor structs the binding never hands across the boundary: it builds frozen JavaScript objects from the fields instead, so there is no C structure to zero and none to compare. Calling native to decide whether two JavaScript objects are equal would add a handle and an error path to an operation with neither

hot-plug subscription, the synthetic raise routes that drive it, and the test reset. The events would need a native callback rooted for the game's life to deliver into JavaScript, and CNA offers no way to enumerate devices *as they change* other than re-reading the inventory above -- which a consumer can already do each frame at no cost. Deferred as plumbing whose only consumer would be the polling this package already exposes

GetHashCode, GetType().Name and Equals for the media value types. Each is implemented exactly in TypeScript over the identity the binding assigns -- a song's file path, an album's name -- and routing them through native would make two objects that are the same media item hash differently depending on which side answered

per-item disposal for handles that never leave the bridge. The snapshot walks CNA's whole graph inside one call and hands JavaScript copied values, so a consumer owns nothing to dispose; each handle's own rule is obeyed on the C side, where CNA's two conventions -- a song out of a collection is a new handle to release, an album out of one is borrowed and must not be -- can each be followed exactly once

backs Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Media.MediaLibrary and the media value types, which this package now populates from CNA's index of the user's Music and Pictures folders rather than reporting empty. Measured: with one WAV planted in XDG_MUSIC_DIR, CNA reports one song, one album and one artist, and a cover.png beside it becomes real album art. Relationships come back as *names* -- two handles for one song never compare equal -- so the managed graph interns by name to give a consumer the object identity XNA implies

backs GraphicsResource's Name, Tag, IsDisposed, GraphicsDevice, ToString, Dispose and the Disposing event. Every one of them works -- measured on a real Texture2D handle: set_name succeeds, the name reads back, is_disposed answers, and get_graphics_device returns the device the texture was made on. They are not bound because this package's GraphicsResource state is authoritative and in TypeScript, so binding them would give one resource two Names and two Tags with nothing to reconcile them; XNA's Tag is a managed object of any type and CNA's is a uint64, so the two cannot even hold the same value. Deferred for that, not for want of a working route
CNA's service-container extensions, which name the two services the runtime registers because C cannot key a container by a C++ type

backs GameComponent, DrawableGameComponent and GameComponentCollection, which this package implements exactly in TypeScript with a unit suite over ordering, mutation, filtering, services and disposal. CNA's header states that a game owns exactly one component collection, so binding these would put a second collection on the same game and make Game.Components.Count and cna_game_components_get_count two counts of one thing. Adopting CNA's instead is not an alternative: a component is a class the consumer subclasses in TypeScript, and CNA's takes C callbacks, so every Update and Draw would cross the boundary twice and the ordering semantics would move to CNA -- for no capability the managed collection lacks

KeyboardState's value semantics -- construction from a key list, key lookup, equality, hash and ToString. XNA's KeyboardState is a value type with no failure mode, and this package implements it exactly; calling native to compare two of them would add a handle and an error path to an operation that has neither

backs Keyboard.GetState(PlayerIndex), which is projected through cna_keyboard_get_state instead. Not an assumption: measured, the per-player route returns a bit-identical snapshot to the plain one, because CNA has one keyboard and its header says every slot reports the same state. The only thing the overload adds is refusing an out-of-range slot, and XNA does not refuse one
scancode and key-name translation, which XNA 4.0 has no counterpart for

backs a projected Microsoft.Xna.Framework member; the adapter already reaches this header's family through at least one imported route, so the remaining declarations are further overloads, accessors and finer-grained spellings of surface the binding covers
rules.unreachedReason: backs projected or projectable XNA surface in a header the adapter imports nothing from, so the whole family is measured and deferred rather than partially covered
